name: Ivan Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. This is confidential. What happens during a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and manage seven people who buy fuel for a large delivery company’s depots. We compare supplier offers, watch tank levels and settle a call when a depot says its delivery is short. I have done this job for eight years and am about average among the managers. I like finding that a driver can leave with a full tank as promised; I dislike explaining a price decision to a depot after I missed a clause.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and how much money can you fall back on?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife, Camila, runs a small bakery, and our children are nine and sixteen. We have a mortgage, my pay is high for this job, and between savings and the bakery we have about ten months of expenses set aside. There are plenty of similar company offices nearby. I have a bachelor’s degree and use AI now and then to compare fuel quotes after another buyer has checked it; I prefer an actual delivery note to a neat forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team to keep the delivery note next to the price quote. A small tool can save an hour, but it cannot put fuel in the depot tank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job should carry on, and the ten-month reserve lets Camila and me handle a slow bakery month. I would keep learning the supplier clauses rather than chase every new screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep our Thursday supplier review and compare any AI price suggestion with the signed delivery record. In the first year we would keep paying an extra 220 monthly against the mortgage only when bakery wages and our reserve are covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about work and home. The main danger is still a missed delivery, not a machine taking my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when a depot says the tank is short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I call the driver and check the meter slip before approving the invoice. The delivery note cannot feed a truck if the tank is empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why make the extra mortgage payment conditional?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Camila’s bakery buys flour and pays two workers before we pay extra to the bank. I would not raid that cash to hit a debt target.

say: I’d keep **delivery notes** beside fuel quotes.
A small tool cannot replace a **real tank check**.
I’d call the **depot driver** before approving a disputed fuel invoice.
think: My **manager role** looks steady in a plateau.
The **ten-month reserve** protects a slow bakery month.
I can spend the quiet year learning **supplier clauses** properly.
do: Keep the **Thursday supplier review** and compare AI prices with signed deliveries.
Overpay the **mortgage by 220** only after flour, bakery payroll and the ten-month reserve are covered.
S0.quote: The delivery note cannot feed a truck if the tank is empty.
fieldNote: He uses AI **occasionally** after another buyer checks it.

Mortgage overpayment waits for **bakery payroll** and reserve protection.

steps.text: Keep Thursday fuel supplier reviews and verify AI prices against signed deliveries
Overpay mortgage 220 monthly only after flour staff wages and ten-month reserve are covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say buying, checking and planning fuel will be among the first tasks a tool takes. I’d want our depots to see wrong delivery alerts before anyone removes a buyer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One purchasing desk might cover several depots, and my manager role could be combined with another. We have money behind us, but a new office may be automating its buying too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This quarter I’d ask my lead buyer to test the new price tool on fifty old orders and record wrong tank estimates. In the first year I’d take the paid supplier-system training once the depot results are sound, and ask Camila whether I can work two paid bakery mornings if her order book needs help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about being made the spare manager, though the reserve buys time. I would rather count a bakery morning as work only when it pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the bakery mornings really pay you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if Camila’s accounts show orders and wages for me after her two staff are paid. I would not take flour money out of another worker’s envelope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you follow the tool if the buyer found errors?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I’d keep the old review until the delivery estimates matched the meter slips.

say: I’d show **wrong tank alerts** before removing buyers from any depot contract.
Fuel buying and planning are **early exposed tasks** across my team.
think: One purchasing desk might cover several depots and remove **my manager role**.
A nearby office may automate its buying too, despite our **cash reserve**.
do: Ask a buyer to test **fifty old orders** for wrong estimates.
Complete **paid supplier training** only after sound results; take bakery mornings only when payroll supports them.
feel: I feel **anxious** about my post but have savings.
S1.quote: I would not take flour money out of another worker’s envelope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the company for closure dates and a named person to settle a short fuel delivery. I would tell the depots not to trust an automated approval over a meter reading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 could buy, plan and check fuel better than I do, so I expect my post to go. Camila’s hands-on baking may last until robots arrive around 2031, but the bakery’s wages vary and my high salary pays much of our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week Camila and I would stop the planned second delivery van and keep its deposit for household bills. Before 2028 I’d ask her accountant whether the bakery could pay me for actual morning shifts without cutting anyone else, and request written severance terms; in the first year after AGI, I’d take those paid shifts only if the accounts and childcare rota support them while I search posted work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed about the wage drop. Ten months of savings give us room to decide, but they do not turn a bakery’s small payroll into my old salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the bakery cannot pay you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not show up as unpaid family labour and call it a plan. I’d use the reserve for a search among nearby employers, knowing their buying desks may face the same AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain the van decision to the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say we are keeping the house sound before buying another business vehicle. The bakery can keep using the van it has.

say: I’d demand **closure dates** and a human fuel contact.
A depot should trust **meter readings** over automatic approval.
think: I **expect my buying role** to go in 2028.
Bakery baking faces **2031 robots**, and its varied pay cannot replace my salary.
do: Stop the **second van purchase** and keep its deposit.
Check **bakery payroll** before taking shifts, while seeking paid jobs after 2028.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about a large wage loss.
S2.quote: I would not show up as unpaid family labour and call it a plan.
fieldNote: His desk work faces the **2028 thinking deadline**.
The bakery must fund **real wages** without cutting existing staff.
He sees its physical baking exposed to **2031 robots**.

steps.text: Cancel the planned second bakery van and keep its deposit for household bills
Ask bakery accountant whether actual shifts can pay him after existing staff wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years lets firms tell buyers which posts remain and let families test other paid work. I would ask for written severance, not a handshake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could use those years to see if the bakery can pay me for hands-on work before 2031. Its ordering and schedules still face AGI in 2031, while the ovens and physical work face robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I’d work one paid bakery morning a month only if Camila’s order book and two workers’ wages are covered, and I’d record the hours and sales. Before 2031 I’d apply for posted bakery production roles nearby only if their written wage covers our mortgage share; after AGI, I’d keep paid kitchen shifts only while the bakery can fund them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, but five years lets us read real accounts instead of guessing. I would not trade my salary for flour-dusted optimism.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train as a baker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Camila would show me the early mix, but I would only take regular shifts after I can do the work and the accounts pay me. I will not call being married to a baker a qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you abandon the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Orders that pay everyone except me. I would keep the depot job while it exists and look at other posted positions.

Families need **paid evidence** before changing work.
Firms should name which **buyer posts** really remain.
think: Physical baking faces **2034 robots** after that.
I can test **paid kitchen work** before leaving my buying salary.

Apply for **posted production work** only at written mortgage-share pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade gives a family time to pay down debt and a firm time to offer honest terms. I would not call a new title a safe job by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 in 2036, and both children would be grown. We could reduce the mortgage if the delivery company and bakery keep paying us. Bakery ordering and my buying desk face 2036 AGI, with hands-on baking robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In January 2027 Camila and I would keep a 300 monthly mortgage overpayment only while bakery staff wages, household bills and ten months of savings remain covered. I’d take two paid production shifts each quarter only if customer orders fund them, then apply for a posted bakery role before 2036 only if the written wage covers our mortgage share; after AGI, I’d remain only while paid human production work exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the eventual job change but able to test it slowly. I would rather hand my wife Camila a wage sheet than a grand plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you borrow to buy another bakery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. One kitchen has to pay its people and our mortgage before I would even discuss a second lease.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger child about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say an apprenticeship can be good if the employer pays and teaches a real skill. I would not choose their trade for them.

say: I’d seek **honest job terms** before changing work.
A new title is not **guaranteed safety**.
Families could use a decade to **pay down debt**.
think: Our **mortgage** could shrink if both the delivery company and bakery keep paying us.
Bakery ordering and my buying desk face **2036 AGI** before 2039 robots reach hands-on baking.
do: Overpay **300 monthly** only after payroll, household bills and reserve are covered.
Take **paid quarterly shifts** only with orders, then seek a written mortgage-share wage.
Remain in **bakery production** after 2036 only while the business funds paid human shifts.
feel: I feel **uneasy** but can test bakery work slowly.

Bakery office tasks remain exposed at **2036 AGI**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my high fuel-buying wage could end before the bakery can pay another worker. Written severance and clear time to test paid production shifts would help. I would not ask Camila to cut her staff’s wages to make room for me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who checks a short fuel delivery when a buying system approves the invoice. A depot cannot run trucks on a perfect invoice and an empty tank.

headlineQuote: A depot cannot run trucks on a perfect invoice and an empty tank.
portrait: **Ivan**, 43, is an experienced fuel-buying manager with a bachelor’s degree.
High pay and **ten months saved** support a mortgage and two children.
He uses AI **occasionally** after colleagues prove it against deliveries.
He tests **paid bakery shifts** only when orders cover existing staff and his wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his high buying wage before the family bakery can pay him.
whatWouldHelp: **Written severance** and time to test genuinely paid kitchen shifts would help.
